content: Dental caries is a widespread chronic condition that affects a significant portion of the global population. It has been hypothesized that xylitol consumption may help prevent dental caries. However, the evidence regarding the effectiveness of xylitol-containing products remains unclear, necessitating a comprehensive review to evaluate their efficacy and safety. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of various xylitol-containing products in preventing dental caries in both children and adults. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science Conference Proceedings, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, up to August 14, 2014. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through the US National Institutes of Health Trials Register and the WHO Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date. Randomized controlled trials evaluating the effects of xylitol products on dental caries in children and adults were included. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Missing data or clarifications were sought from study authors when feasible. For continuous outcomes, mean differences and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, while dichotomous outcomes were reported as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs. Prevented fractions (PFs) and their 95% CIs were used to summarize the percentage reduction in caries. A fixed-effect model was employed for meta-analyses involving fewer than four studies, with plans to use a random-effects model for larger meta-analyses. The review included 10 studies involving a total of 5,903 participants. Of these, one study was deemed to have a low risk of bias, two had an unclear risk of bias, and seven were assessed as having a high risk of bias. The primary finding was that fluoride toothpaste containing 10% xylitol may reduce caries by 13% over 2.5 to 3 years compared to fluoride-only toothpaste (PF -0.13, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.08, based on data from 4,216 children, low-quality evidence). However, the remaining evidence from small, single studies with significant risk of bias and uncertainty in effect estimates was insufficient to confirm any benefit of xylitol products in children. One study reported that xylitol syrup (8 g/day) reduced caries by 58% (95% CI 33% to 83%, based on 94 infants, low-quality evidence) compared to a low-dose xylitol syrup (2.67 g/day) consumed over one year. Other findings, such as the effects of xylitol lozenges, sucking tablets, tablets, or wipes in children and infants, were based on very low-quality evidence, with 95% CIs that were compatible with both a reduction and an increase in caries. Similarly, a single study on xylitol lozenges in adults provided low-quality evidence, with effect estimates also compatible with both a reduction and an increase in caries. Regarding adverse effects, four studies reported no adverse effects from xylitol interventions, while two studies noted similar rates of adverse effects between study groups. Other studies either mentioned adverse effects without providing usable data or did not address them at all. Reported adverse effects included mouth sores, abdominal cramps, bloating, constipation, flatulence, and loose stools or diarrhea. In conclusion, there is low-quality evidence suggesting that fluoride toothpaste containing xylitol may be more effective than fluoride-only toothpaste in preventing caries in the permanent teeth of children, with no associated adverse effects. However, this finding should be interpreted cautiously due to the high risk of bias and the fact that it is based on two studies conducted by the same authors in the same population. The remaining evidence is of low to very low quality and is insufficient to determine whether other xylitol-containing products can prevent caries in infants, older children, or adults.
